title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Compliance Evidence, and Risk/Exceptions
author: Jordan Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls and operational procedures for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC), incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk & exceptions. It is intended for engineering, security, compliance, and operations teams as the authoritative reference for implementation and evidence collection.

Scope
Applies to all production services, private deployments (VPC/on-prem), Dedicated fleet control plane, and the Redwood Console. Where cloud-specific controls are required, the document highlights AWS/GCP/Azure examples while keeping control objectives cloud-agnostic.

Summary of changes
- Formalized RBAC role matrix and onboarding checklist (v1.0)
- Standardized audit log pipeline and retention tiers
- SDLC security gates for model onboarding and runtime changes
- Incident response evidence preservation steps to support audits and legal holds
- Exception and temporary risk approval workflow

1) RBAC and Authentication

Goals
- Principle of least privilege for humans and service identities
- Consistent role definitions across Control Plane, Data Plane, and Console
- Short-lived credentials, strong MFA enforcement, and automated access reviews

Role model (high level)
- org-admin: Full administrative access to customer account configurations and billing (restricted to named principals)
- security-admin: Manage security policies, IAM roles, audit log access, and compliance evidence
- infra-operator: Manage infra provisioning, terraform state, cloud accounts, and capacity (no PII access by default)
- dev-engineer: Deploy and operate services; requires scoped access to CI/CD artifacts and runtime logs subject to RBAC
- svc-account: Machine/service identities used by runtime components; bound to least privilege scopes

Onboarding and offboarding checklist
1. Request via access request system (Jira Service Desk / internal access portal) with business justification and expiration date.
2. Owner (team lead) approves; security-admin performs risk review for high privilege roles.
3. Provision role with time-bound certificate or short-lived token; enable MFA for human accounts.
4. Record grant in access registry with metadata: principal, role, owner, justification, expiry.
5. Offboard: revoke active sessions, remove role bindings, and update registry.

Periodic reviews
- Quarterly automated access review for org-admin, security-admin roles.
- Annual review for all infra-operator and dev-engineer roles.
- Automated deprovisioning reminders 7 days before expiry.

Authentication and secrets
- Enforce SSO (OIDC or SAML) integration (Okta) with SCIM provisioning.
- Enforce MFA for all human accounts.
- Secrets stored in KMS or managed Secret Manager; secrets rotation policy: 90 days for user-facing credentials, 30 days for service keys unless automated rotation is in place.

2) Audit Logging

Objectives
- Provide tamper-evident logs for authentication, authorization changes, config changes, runtime errors, data access, and deployment events.
- Support for forensic analysis, compliance evidence, and anomaly detection.

Log types and minimum retention
| Log type | Examples | Retention (default) | Retention (regulated customers) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| AuthN/AuthZ | SSO logins, MFA events, role grants/revokes | 1 year | 7 years (as contract requires) |
| Admin/config changes | IAM policy changes, routing policy updates | 2 years | 7 years |
| API access logs | Customer API requests (metadata only) | 180 days | Customer-specific as contract |
| System/daemon logs | Runtime errors, crash reports (no PII) | 90 days | 2 years |
| Audit trail for data access | Data plane reads/writes to customer data stores | 2 years | As required by customer SLA |

Implementation notes
- Control plane relies on cloud provider audit (CloudTrail / Cloud Audit Logs) combined with an internal event bus that writes to an append-only S3/GCS bucket with object-level immutability (where available) and object locks for retention enforcement.
- Logs are shipped to SIEM (Splunk/Elastic/Chronicle) via secure forwarders with TLS and mutual auth.
- All critical logs are checksum-signed and hashed into a WORM-backed store for tamper evidence.
- Access to audit logs is RBAC-protected and logged; only security-admin and designated auditors have read access to raw audit buckets.

Alerting and monitoring
- Alerting thresholds: >5 failed org-admin login attempts in 10 minutes; unexpected changes to IAM policies; creation of new org-admin principals.
- All alerts escalate to oncall security and SRE teams via PagerDuty.

3) Data Residency and Retention

Principles
- Respect customer-configured region limits; data must remain in specified regions for storage, backups, and audit logs unless an exception is approved.
- Minimize retention of customer data to what is required for operation and compliance.

Residency controls
- Deployment overlays: service config supports regional overlays that pin data plane storage to specific cloud regions (e.g., eu-west-1, us-east-1).
- Backup and DR: backups inherit region tag; cross-region replication is disabled by default unless explicitly requested and contractually allowed.

Retention policy (default tiers)
- Customer operational data (metadata, config): 2 years
- Customer-generated content (model inputs/outputs): default 90 days; configurable per-customer down to 7 days for strict privacy customers
- Audit logs: see Audit Logging table above

Data deletion and verification
1. Deletion request received (customer or support).
2. Run deletion workflow: remove objects from primary stores, clear caches and KV stores, and trigger background compaction to purge tombstones.
3. Generate deletion report: list of object keys and locations, deletion timestamps, and verification hash.
4. For sensitive deletions subject to legal hold, preserve hashes and metadata in secure evidence store; do not remove until legal hold is lifted.

4) Secure SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle)

Objective
- Integrate security gates into all stages of development for services and model onboarding to reduce vulnerabilities and prevent regressions in production.

Gates and tools
- Design phase: Threat modeling required for any change affecting authentication, data flow, or model outputs that handle PII. Template required and stored in design repo.
- Code phase: Mandatory code review, static analysis (Semgrep/CodeQL), and dependency scanning (Snyk or equivalent).
- Build phase: Reproducible builds, artifact signing, SBOM generation.
- Pre-deploy: Automated integration tests, canary and chaos experiments in staging, and runtime security scanners (fuzzing for model inference paths where applicable).
- Release: Signed release artifact, rollout policy with automatic rollback threshold (error rate >1% or latency SLO breach for 5 minutes).

Model onboarding specific controls
- Data provenance review for model training data: ensure no customer PII was included unless contracted.
- Model card and evaluation summary required.
- Quantization and kernel changes documented and included in performance/quality checks.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Goals
- Detect, contain, eradicate, and recover while preserving evidence and maintaining legal/compliance obligations.

Roles and responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): usually security lead on-call until incident triaged.
- Forensics lead: performs evidence capture and preserves chain of custody.
- Communications lead: customer/legal/comms coordination.
- SRE/Engineering responders: mitigations, rollbacks, and remediation.

High-level incident procedure
1. Detection & Triage: use SIEM alerts, automated monitors, customer reports. Classify severity (P1-P4) by impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
2. Containment: isolate affected instances, revoke compromised keys, apply emergency rules to block exfiltration.
3. Evidence preservation: snapshot VMs, export relevant logs (auth, API, network) to a secure evidence store with write-once retention, and document time-stamped actions.
4. Investigation: forensics lead and engineering debug, collect root cause and blast radius.
5. Remediation & Recovery: apply fixes, rotate keys, rebuild images.
6. Post-incident: produce postmortem with timelines, impact, root cause, and follow-up action items tied to owners and deadlines.

Evidence handling and legal holds
- All preserved evidence is stored with metadata (collector, timestamp, hash, justification).
- Legal or customer-required holds must be recorded; evidence retention extended to hold duration.
- Chain of custody log updated for each access.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Control mapping and evidence catalog
- Maintain a control/evidence catalog that maps each compliance control (e.g., SOC2 CC, ISO 27001 A.9, HIPAA relevant controls) to one or more artifacts: runbooks, configs, audit logs, test results, screenshots, and attestations.

Automation and playbooks
- Automated evidence collectors run quarterly and on-demand to snapshot relevant artifacts into a compliance evidence bucket with versioned exports.
- Evidence is annotated with control IDs, collection time, and responsible owner.
- Manual evidence (e.g., signed policies, vendor attestations) are uploaded to the evidence repository and referenced in the catalog.

Evidence retention and access
- Standard evidence retention: 7 years for SOC2/enterprise customers; 2 years for internal operational evidence.
- Access governed by RBAC; auditors granted time-bound access tokens tied to specific evidence sets and logged.

7) Risk and Exceptions

Temporary exceptions
- Exception request required when a required control cannot be met for business reasons (e.g., legacy on-prem connector, customer requirement preventing automated rotation).
- Exception request must include: control impacted, business justification, compensating controls, risk score (low/medium/high), owner, and expiry date (max 90 days for high risk).

Approval flow
1. Requester opens exception ticket in compliance queue with required fields.
2. Security reviews and assesses compensating controls.
3. If risk <= medium, security-admin can approve with mitigating controls and monitoring.
4. If risk is high, approval requires CISO and affected product VP sign-off.
5. Each approved exception is tracked, monitored, and re-evaluated weekly until closure.

Permanent risk acceptance
- For risks that cannot be fully mitigated, a formal risk acceptance memo is required, outlining business rationale, residual risk, and executive sign-off. These memos are stored in the risk register and reviewed at least annually.
